question: In Oradea, Romania, the local government initiated eviction proceedings against the leader of the Nagyváradhegyfok Premonstratensian Provostry, Rudolf Anzelm Fejes O. Praem., Premonstratensian provost-prelate, despite the provostry and its associated properties being recognised and registered ecclesiastical legal entities and assets by the Romanian state.

The central authorities of the Romanian state officially recognise and finance the provostry, while the Oradea local government lists the building complex in its EU-funded renovation project (SMIS 316653) as a ‘former Premonstratensian monastery’, thereby challenging the institution’s legal status.

This contradictory situation between the state authorities raises concerns regarding rule of law, legal certainty, respect for vested rights and the prohibition of abuse of rights, particularly concerning the lawful use of EU funding. There is a suspicion that the financing documentation does not adequately reflect the officially recognised ecclesiastical institution associated with the properties. 1.
Does this situation raise suspicion of an irregularity under Article 2(30) of Regulation (EU) 2021/1060?

Will the Commission examine whether Article 17 TFEU, as well as Articles 10 and 47 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights, have been violated, and whether the Romanian authorities’ actions justify initiating infringement proceedings under Article 258 TFEU?

Will the Commission examine whether this internal incoherence affects the proper financial management of the EU budget and whether it raises the applicability of the regime of conditionality for rule of law under Regulation (EU, Euratom) 2020/2092?
answer: 1. Under shared management, Member States should prevent and address irregularities in EU-funded projects, ensuring also compliance with the fundamental rights as enshrined in the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union (the Charter).

After assessments by Romania’s Managing Authority, based on Regulation (EU) 2021/1060 (1) and national law, no financial irregularities, fraud, conflict of interest, false declarations or incomplete documentation were found in relation to the implementation of the EU-funded project concerned. 2. The EU has no general competence to regulate religious matters.

Article 17(1) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union provides that the Union respects and does not prejudice the status of churches and religious associations under national law. In addition, the provisions of the Charter apply to Member States only when implementing EU law (2).

In all other cases, national authorities, including national courts, bear the primary responsibility for ensuring compliance with fundamental rights in accordance with national and international legal obligations. 3.

The application of the Rule of Law Conditionality Regulation (3) is subject to specific conditions, including the existence of a sufficiently direct link between the breach of rule of law principles and the EU budget, as well as the absence of more effective protection of the EU budget through other procedures established by EU legislation.

Based on the information currently available, the conditions for applying the regulation do not appear to be met. The Commission nevertheless continues to monitor developments in all Member States and anyone can submit relevant information through the dedicated complaint form (4).
